Phish News
Phish, TAB Make Cameo Appearance At Higher Ground
Source: Phantasy Tour
Posted by: dgreenhaus
Posted on: 2004-04-12 10:08:19 ET
Last Updated: 2004-04-12 11:31:36 ET

Last night, April 11, during a Grippo Funk Band show at Higher Ground
in Winooski, Vermont, the individual members of Phish emerged at
different times, eventually settling in for "Chalkdust Torture".

After setbreak, Dave Grippo's band, which includes Andy Moroz and
Jennifer Hartswick, returned to the stage, complete with Trey Anastasio
on guitar, Russ Lawton on drums, Tony Markellis on bass and Ray
Paczkowski on keyboards. At this point, the current, on-stage line-up
was only 3 members shy of the full 10-piece Trey Anastasio Band (TAB).
The unit then launched into the TAB staples Push on Till The Day and
Drifting. Trey then invited Page McConnell to join Ray on keys for a
rendition of Bob Marley's Small Axe, yet another song TAB has played.

Jon Fishman then emerged to join the band for both Last Tube and Dire
Straits' Sultans of Swing. And finally, Mike Gordon joined in for a
monsterous version of Sand featuring all the members of Phish with the
7-piece TAB, during which the TAB members filetered off the stage
leaving only the members of Phish remaining.

With just the members of Phish on stage, and a crowd in a frenzy, the
band launched into Chalkdust Torture, after which Jon, Page and Mike
left the stage, and Jen, Tony, Russ and Ray returned for Flock of Words.
Andy then returned for Plasma. The set concluded with the members of
Phish retaking the stage with TAB to cover Stevie Wonder's Higher
Ground.

tags.notes: This was the first show of the Coventry festival and was simulcast in movie theaters nationwide. During YEM, the band gave away their trampolines. Throughout the duration of the set, groups of fans held the trampolines above their heads, and some fans jumped on the trampolines as well. During Hood, Trey (speaking in rhythm) noted that because there were a row of rocks separating the band from the crowd, they were feeling a certain level of disconnect (particularly when Mike plays a "sexy" note). To remedy the situation, Trey and Mike ventured down onto the rocks for the duration of the song. At the end of Hood, the band stopped playing, allowing the audience to sing the "You can feel good, good, good about Hood" refrain.

0.notes: Jam breaks from the standard at 11:00 into a mellow groove that builds energy and > to "Runaway Jim."

1.notes: Very improvisational, "Type II" version with a -> to a very improvisational, "Type II" "Gotta Jibboo."

2.notes: The yang to 4/16/04's yin. Tight playing for '04. Dark and grimy up front, but once it pushes through to the heavens this "Gotta Jibboo" is breathtaking.

3.notes: The band gave away their trampolines. Throughout the duration of the set, groups of fans held the trampolines above their heads, and some fans jumped on the trampolines as well.

7.notes: Jam segment rages practically non-stop, and Tom Marshall assists with the "Rocco" lyrics

9.notes: Nimbly textured and surgically precise like the big '97 "Bags?" No. Highly improvisational, well played AND a great listen? Absolutely. This version is MUST-HEAR, like 11/21/97, 12/30/97 and 9/14/99. The Coventry "Bag" is full of "2.0-style jamming," is played very well overall, and it's highly listenable. -> to "46 Days."

13.notes: Trey talks about writing "David Bowie" for 4 1/2 minutes before the song - well worth hearing. The jam itself is pretty decent with a nice little shift to major mode and an intense ending.

Trey told a story of the summer he spent living in a cabin in the Northeast Kingdom where he remembered writing several songs, including Bowie. Trey explained that Bowie was an attempt to see "how far can you push it in the harmonic and rhythmic language and still have people dancing."

15.notes: A decent jam develops which has an underlying Mike and Fish fueled groove that continues almost throughout. Trey at times uses a lot of distortion, and his seeming lack of direction gives the jam a disjointed feel. Great -> to "The Wedge."

17.notes: While the composed section is far from spotless, the jam is very good and multi-dimensional, including a nice move to major mode followed by some great exploration. Unfinished with a > to "Free."

18.notes: Some sweet Mike bass, then gets very quiet with just Mike and Trey playing, then Fish and Page jump back in

20.notes: Very raw in parts (at least Trey), but a serious piece of improvisation nonetheless.  At the 7 minute mark, the band gets very quiet and almost stops.  Trey plays solo for a stretch, and briefly addresses the crowd.  Around 12:30, the other band mates rejoin in a very upbeat and rocking jam that accelerates into near fury by 21:30.

22.notes: Trey (speaking in rhythm) noted that because there were a row of rocks separating the band from the crowd, they were feeling a certain level of disconnect (particularly when Mike plays a "sexy" note). To remedy the situation, Trey and Mike ventured down onto the rocks for the duration of the song. At the end, the band stopped playing, allowing the audience to sing the "You can feel good, good, good about Hood" refrain.

tags.notes: This was the second show of the Coventry festival and was the presumed "Final Show." When Trey made his "break-up" announcement the preceding May, he indicated that Coventry would be the final Phish shows. In reality, this turned out to be the final public show for over four and a half years. This show was simulcast in movie theaters nationwide. There was a fireworks display between the end of the third set and the encore. There was no P.A. music after The Curtain With.

3.notes: Trey announced that, for the first time in 21 years, he was nervous performing a Phish show.

6.notes: Extremely improvisational version which leaves "CDT" behind near the end and -> to "Possum."

Trey reveals that the Wolfman's Brother is actually Fish

10.notes: Very unusual version. The first jam segment is strange, spacey, and Trey sounds off-key at times. Then there's a second jam following the closing riff (without vocal refrain) which has some interesting moments and is pretty soulful.
Trey briefly played his guitar with a glow stick

13.notes: The band expresses their gratitude to the audience

14.notes: Skip the composed section (ugly) and go straight to the jam (released on Live Bait Vol. 5), which is excellent, extended and improvisational. The final 6 spacey minutes are a combination of sad, eerie and haunting, with a hint of optimism near the end. Unfinished with a -> to "Ghost." One of many great jams from the morass of Coventry.

15.notes: Through a crack in the fabric of space-time a horde of flaming orange locusts cascaded down the fetid slope of manure, became a cyclone of debris, limbs, and offal in the muddy bowl then coalesced into a sheet of light which rapidly withdrew upslope back into the void of infinity. [-> in from a strong "SOAM." The jam breaks into an angry, rocking groove that grows dissonant, tension-filled, and includes Trey's eerie yelling and digi-guitar effects.]
There was an enormous glow stick war featuring hundreds, if not thousands, of orange glow sticks.

17.notes: All of the band members sporadically shouted "Seven Below" throughout the jam.

19.notes: Blistering, fierce, machine-gun Trey, akin at times to Hendrix at his best!

20.notes: Trey works in some music theory banter
Contained alternate lyrics honoring monitor mixer, Mark "Bruno" Bradley.

21.notes: Spontaneously created and included lyrics in honor of production manager, Hadden Hipsley, and tour accountant, Richard Glasgow (a.k.a. Dickie Scotland).

22.notes: Trey asked the crowd to sing to another of their friends "for the last time."

24.notes: Trey talks about writing The Curtain and thanks the audience

25.notes: Trey stopped and restarted the jam segment because they were in the wrong key or, as he explained, "Since we are going to be bringing ourselves back in time, we may as well do it in the correct key."
